beats.lead: Ask a computer for a random number
beats.text: It runs a formula and reads you the next line of a script.
beats.note: Same starting seed, same sequence, every time. Nothing is chosen; it is all pre-computed. That is why they are called pseudo-random.

beats.name: John von Neumann
beats.role: He built the first computer method for it (square a number, keep the middle digits, repeat) for Monte Carlo runs on ENIAC. He also warned exactly what it was.

beats.text: Anyone who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin.
beats.note: His point: no formula is truly random. He used them anyway (hundreds of times faster than reading random numbers off punch cards), knowing precisely what they were.

beats.lead: And his method could trap itself
beats.text: Hit the wrong number and it spits zeros forever.
beats.note: The middle-square method can collapse to zero, or fall into a short loop, and never recover. Von Neumann counted that a virtue: a failure you can at least catch.

beats.text: Even an AI's flashes of randomness are a formula quietly choosing the next number.

beats.line: A computer can fake chance. It cannot roll a die.
